does_not_mean: There is no space: 'town' and 'quarter' label groups of states, not places
Cafés are not agents; nothing chooses to open or close
It does not say which process is more real, more organised or better
explanation: Two towns can have exactly the same number of cafés open on an average day. In one, each café stays open for years; in the other, cafés open and close every week in a busy quarter while the quiet quarter hardly changes. Counting open cafés on a random day cannot tell the towns apart. Following one café over time can.
illustrative_status: illustrative only; matches the qualitative content of CL-T88/F8N and GT-F78, not their numbers

mapping.object: a stochastic process (its generator)

mapping.object: stationary occupancy / prevalence pi(A)

mapping.figure: how long one café stays open
mapping.object: entrance-episode lifetime L = pi(A)/J_A

mapping.figure: a busy quarter where cafés open and close every week
mapping.object: states with high total transition rate

misleading_readings: Reading the long-lived town as 'more organised': in GT's PCOMP the long life comes from uneven activity, with no structural preference at all (GT-F78)
title: Two towns with the same number of open cafés

does_not_mean: Memory is not a mind and nothing is remembered unless the model declares an augmented state
The diary is not stored anywhere in the substrate unless it is part of the declared state
It says nothing about physical time
explanation: Sometimes a photograph of the present is all you need to forecast what happens next. Sometimes two identical photographs lead to different futures, and only the diary tells them apart: then history is a predictive variable. A historian can read a diary without the diary changing anything; a council that acts on the diary is different. Only the second makes history part of the rules.

mapping.figure: a photograph of the present
mapping.object: the complete current state x

mapping.figure: a diary of recent events
mapping.object: a history register h (augmented state)

mapping.figure: a forecast of the next event
mapping.object: the conditional law of the next transition

mapping.figure: a photograph good enough that the diary adds nothing
mapping.object: Markov (predictive) sufficiency of the state for the declared observable

mapping.figure: a historian reading the diary versus a council acting on it
mapping.object: a trajectory observable versus a rule that reads history (CL's H axis)

misleading_readings: Thinking more diary is always better: beyond the sufficient register, extra history adds nothing (CL predictive quotients)
Thinking a long diary means long memory: in irreducible chains information about the initial state decays
title: A photograph and a diary

does_not_mean: Nobody is playing: moves happen at random rates and no one decides them
It does not say one clock is the true one
explanation: In a board game where moves happen at random rates, whether the white pieces or the black pieces finish first can depend on whether you count minutes or moves. That is GT's clock dependence: the same sequence of moves, weighted differently. If you also stop recording the moves of one kind of piece, the record you keep can look as if it remembers things the full game does not: that is CL's epoch, which hides events as well as changing the clock.

mapping.figure: minutes on a wall clock
mapping.object: continuous model time

mapping.figure: the number of moves made
mapping.object: jump (event) count

mapping.figure: counting only the moves of one kind of piece
mapping.object: CL's pair-event epoch: a time change plus a projection that hides triad events

misleading_readings: Treating CL's and GT's clock effects as one phenomenon (X::0003 records the contrast)
title: Counting minutes or counting moves

does_not_mean: Rooms and doors are not space: they label states and transitions
Nobody pushes the door; there are no forces
It does not say every observable is continuous
explanation: A door that gets heavier is used less and less, and some counts of use slide smoothly toward what happens when it is locked. But locking it is different in kind: some routes stop existing, and some changes can no longer be undone. Forbidding is not just extreme discouragement, even when a few numbers look continuous.

mapping.figure: a heavier and heavier door
mapping.object: a soft suppression factor 1/2, 1/4, 1/9, 1/16 on a transition

mapping.figure: a locked door
mapping.object: a hard prohibition (zero rate; outside the log-weight algebra)

mapping.figure: how often the door is used
mapping.object: stationary observables such as flux or partner index

mapping.figure: which rooms can be reached at all
mapping.object: the support and reachable class (one-way transitions)

misleading_readings: Concluding that hard bans are 'just' strong weights (support changes, GT-F51)
Concluding that they are always discontinuous (GT-F54)
title: A heavy door and a locked door

does_not_mean: The committee has no purpose or identity; nobody intends it to continue
Long life is not identity through complete replacement (not defined in E5A)
The chair has no special power in the rules
explanation: A committee can keep meeting for a long time while its members come and go. That is different from a fixed group of people who all have to stay. But a long-running committee does not prove anyone is keeping it together: if members rejoin as fast as they leave, the committee may last simply because everything around the chair is busy.

mapping.object: the anchor vertex c (an observation index, not a privileged entity)

mapping.figure: the committee meets while it has at least two members
mapping.object: the flexible predicate F_2PATH(c): deg(c) >= 2

mapping.figure: a member leaving or joining while the committee still meets
mapping.object: an eligible within-episode turnover toggle (counted by Omega)

mapping.figure: a member who leaves and rejoins at once
mapping.object: flicker: counted twice by Omega, not a replacement

misleading_readings: Reading persistence through turnover as organisation (GT-F78 shows uneven activity can produce it)
Reading Omega as the number of replacements
title: A committee whose members rotate

does_not_mean: People and heights are labels for vertices and degrees; there is no space or body
It does not say any vertex is special
explanation: If you pick the tallest person in a room, they are tall by construction; that tells you nothing about whether height lasts. In these models 'height' (number of links) keeps changing, and whoever was picked drifts back to average. The useful question is how fast, compared with a fair baseline.

mapping.object: the lagged degree gap against a uniformly chosen vertex

mapping.object: exchangeability: no labelled vertex stays distinguished (GT-F72)

misleading_readings: Reading a slow return to average as a lasting centre
title: Picking the tallest person in the room
